issues.issue: The effective date is left blank ("effective as of ____________"), a mechanical gap that leaves the commencement of the instrument unstated on its face.
Section 2.15 defines "Effective Date" as "the date first stated above," but no date is stated above, so the two provisions cannot be operated together.
This recital's "approximately 124 communities" and "approximately 1,392" CAIs are only illustrative against the operative definitions in Sections 2.38 and 2.7, but nothing here purports to bind.
A recital of Network Operator's skill could be read against the express warranties in Section 5.1.6-5.1.8, but the operative warranties plainly govern.
"[A]mong other things" introduces an open-ended recital list of services whose outer boundary is not fixed.
The recital sweeps in functions "otherwise commonly performed by a dark fiber and lit network provider," an industry-custom standard with no stated boundary.

That open-ended recital sits against Section 2.60's definition of Services as "all performance obligations of the Network Operator hereunder" and Section 4.7.1's implied-services clause, which could expand duties beyond the written text.
Article 2 states that all capitalized terms are defined there, yet capitalized terms such as "Termination Date" (Section 3.6.1.1) and "Attachment Database" are used but not defined in Article 2.
"Control" is used to define Affiliate without any ownership or voting threshold, unlike Section 8.1.4 which supplies a 50% test for change of control.
The definition cross-references Section 4.9.2, but the Annual Plan is actually required by Section 4.9.3.2; Section 4.9.2 concerns agreements between MTC and others.
"[A]s the same may be revised from time to time in MTC's sole discretion" leaves the population of CAIs entirely at one party's election, with no stated limit on additions or deletions.
The revision right runs "up until the Commencement Date," yet Section 2.8 fixes the Commencement Date by reference to 90% of "the CAIs" being connected, so each definition depends on the other.
Clause (a) requires both 90% of mileage and 90% of "the CAIs" connected, but the identity of "the CAIs" is fixed only as of the very date being determined.
The definition cannot be squared with Section 2.7, which lets MTC revise the Exhibit A CAI list in its sole discretion up until the Commencement Date, making the 90% measure a moving target.
"[M]ay include, but is not necessarily limited to" makes the enumerated categories illustrative only, leaving the outer boundary of Confidential Information undetermined.
A Dark Fiber Customer leases "from MTC," yet Section 4.7.4.4 contemplates the Network Operator executing dark fiber leases in its own name on Network Operator Network Extensions.
"[T]he date first stated above" points to the preamble, where the date line is blank, so the Effective Date that drives Sections 2.8, 3.1 and 4.9.4 has no stated referent.
The catch-all "other substantial and extraordinary accidents" and "other similar casualty" sit against a long enumerated list, leaving the reach of the general words open to ejusdem generis argument.
"[C]ritical areas of operation and management" is undefined and no KPI set is fixed in the instrument itself, Exhibit E being incomplete.

MBI Network Extensions are defined as funded "in whole or in part" by MTC, while Section 2.42 defines Network Operator Network Extensions to exclude extensions funded by MTC, leaving jointly funded extensions capable of falling in both categories.
The definition mixes a binding scope ("as built or acquired") with descriptive planning figures (1,338 miles, 1,392 CAIs), leaving unclear whether the figures are promissory.

The second sentence is circular: an extension becomes part of the MTC Network "unless it is a Network Extension and the Network Operator establishes ... that it is not or does not become part of the MTC Network," defining the result by the result.
The exclusion of extensions "funded by MTC" overlaps with Section 2.36's MBI Network Extension, which need only be funded in part by MTC, leaving mixed-funding extensions unallocated.
"[S]imilar services" is the sole benchmark for the deemed fee, and no method is given for identifying which Price Schedule item is similar.
"[P]lus any additional policies reasonably required by MTC" lets one party enlarge the defined set at will, against a closed list of presently identified policies.

The definition combines a sweeping catch-all ("[a]ny amounts earned ... other than the categories expressly excluded ... shall be Network Revenue") with enumerated exclusions (w)-(z), leaving the boundary between excluded "value-added services" or "professional services unrelated to the MTC Network" and included revenue contestable.

The exclusion of "revenues earned by a retail Affiliate" must be read with Section 4.8, which allows an Affiliate to be a Third Party Service Provider on non-discriminatory terms, so affiliate transactions can shift revenue out of the sharing base.
Price Caps are said to be "set forth in Exhibit F," but the exhibit list identifies Exhibit D as Price Caps and Exhibit F as the EOPSS/ITD Master Services Agreement.
The Price Schedule must cover "all standard offerings" while custom quotations for "non-standard customer requests" are outside it, with no test for what is standard.

A Renewal Decision must conform "to the requirements of Section 3.2," but Section 3.2 states no requirements for any decision and the defined term appears nowhere in the operative renewal machinery of Sections 3.3-3.5.
Defining Retail Service as "services provided by a Third Party Service Provider" makes the category depend on who provides it rather than what it is.

Because Section 2.64 defines Third Party Service Provider as any organization "other than Network Operator," Section 4.8's prohibition on Network Operator providing Retail Services can never bite as written.
Service Area is defined as a portion of the MTC Network shown on Exhibit C, while Section 2.8 uses the Service Area to measure constructed mileage; no map is reproduced in the instrument.
Defining Services as "all performance obligations of the Network Operator hereunder" is entirely circular and supplies no independent content.
The SLA is defined as an existing agreement, but Section 4.13.1 states the SLA is still "in the process of" completion and Exhibit E is not attached.

The enumerated carrier types are followed by the qualifier "receiving Wholesale Service from the Network Operator," leaving unclear whether that condition limits the whole class or only the last item.

Clause (c) covers "lit transmission service of not less than 10 Gbps to an institutional customer without protocol," a phrase whose grammar leaves "without protocol" and "institutional customer" undefined and ambiguous.
The Term runs to the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date, a date that Sections 2.7 and 2.8 leave contingent on MTC's own revisions to the CAI list.
Section 2.54 defines a Renewal Decision by reference to "the requirements of Section 3.2," yet this Section imposes no requirements on any decision.
A Renewal Request may be made only in a two-month window 30 to 32 months before expiration, with "time being of the essence," but nothing states the consequence of a request made outside the window.

Section 3.6.1.3 and 3.6.1.4 attach very different dark fiber exercise prices to which party "notifies" the other it does not wish to renew during these negotiations, so the unilateral right to terminate negotiations here has price consequences not addressed.
The right is to lease "between four (4) and eight (8) strands" without saying who elects the number within that range or on what basis.
The exclusion turns on strand counts "as of the Termination Date," a capitalized term nowhere defined in Article 2, which states that all capitalized terms are defined there.
The measurement period runs to "the date of the Request for Renewal," using a term that does not match the defined "Renewal Request" and leaving the period undefined if no request is made.
Trigger (c), "upon the expiry of the Term of this Agreement," is on its face satisfied in every case, which would swallow triggers (a), (b) and (d).
If trigger (c) applies to every expiry, this pricing table would displace Section 3.6.1.4, which sets a different price when Network Operator is the party declining renewal.
This table cannot be reconciled with Section 3.6.1.3(c), which makes the more favourable table apply "upon the expiry of the Term" without regard to which party declined renewal.
The cross-reference to "Section 3.6.1.3 or 3.1.6.4" transposes the digits of Section 3.6.1.4, and the adjustment methodology points to Section 4.9.4 rather than the CPI formula in Section 4.9.4.2.

Charging on "the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment regardless of disclaimers" sits awkwardly with Section 3.6.1.11, which excludes disclaimed mileage from IRU fees and voids rights in disclaimed strands.

Payment is due "on or before the end of the Term," yet Section 3.6.1 makes the right arise only "upon expiration of the Term" and after cure of defaults, leaving the price payable before the right is known to exist.
The lease commences "upon termination or expiration of the Term," while Section 3.6.1 grants the right only "upon expiration of the Term" and Section 3.6.2 denies it on termination for cause.
"[A]ny requirements of MTC's policies then applicable to others" and "then-prevailing prices" leave the future terms wholly at MTC's determination.

The formula and its narrative description conflict in expression, and "the last two full calendar year" is ungrammatical, leaving unclear whether one or two years of maintenance cost is the baseline and whether it is halved.

The exclusion of disclaimed mileage from "IRU fees" is difficult to square with Section 3.6.1.5(b), which fixes the exercise price "regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11."

The trailing conjunct "and the Network Operator has invested less than $3,000,000" may qualify only limb (b) or both limbs (a) and (b), which changes whether a for-cause termination alone destroys the rights.
"[R]esponsible for all aspects" is followed by responsibilities that "include, generally," so the enumerated duties neither limit nor define the general obligation.
Subsection 4.1.10.4 requires the Fiber Management Plan draft within six months "of the Effective Date," while Section 4.5.2 measures the same six months from "execution of this Agreement."
"[R]easonably adjusted" supplies no mechanism or measure for the extension of the deliverable deadlines.

A deemed acceptance operates unless a challenge is made within five business days, and the challenge "may be based only on alleged noncompliance with the agreed acceptance testing protocol" — a protocol that Section 4.2.2.5 says is still to be developed.
Reducing "the time periods stated in said Article ... by eighty percent (80%)" does not map onto Article 11's staged 15/30/45-day steps and arbitration timetable.

Network Operator must perform the additional services if MTC requires them while the compensation terms remain to be negotiated as "commercially reasonable terms," leaving price to be settled after performance.
The Ramp-Up Plan "shall include but need not be limited to" the listed elements, so the enumerated items neither exhaust nor bound the required content.
"[S]ervices beyond the scope contemplated herein" and "reasonable accommodation" are undefined boundaries for what ITD and EOPSS may separately engage.
"Contract Price" is capitalized and treated as defined, but no definition of it appears in Article 2 or elsewhere in the Agreement.

The Attachment Database is defined only by reference to a separate Owner's Project Management Services agreement, contrary to Article 2's statement that capitalized terms take their meaning from Article 2.
Compliance is measured against "the then-current version of Exhibit G," implying the exhibit may change without the written amendment Section 12.1 requires.
The six-month deadline runs from "execution of this Agreement," while Section 4.1.10.4 sets the same deliverable six months from the Effective Date.
"[E]xcessive stranded segments of fiber" and "reasonably calculated to optimize use" give MTC approval criteria with no measurable content.
"[E]xcept as otherwise expressly provided in this Section" is self-referential and does not identify which subsection of 4.5 creates the exception.

Sole ownership of Network Operator Network Extensions is hard to square with Section 2.39, under which any fiber extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless Network Operator proves otherwise to MTC's reasonable satisfaction.
Customer ownership of funded extensions sits against Section 2.39, which presumes any extension of the MTC Network becomes part of the MTC Network absent proof to the contrary.
Network Operator is given "the same role and rights ... as are set forth in section 4.2," but Section 4.2 confers only a consultative role during design and construction, not operating rights.
MTC's ownership of every MBI Network Extension "regardless of the source of its funding" conflicts with Section 4.5.6.3, which makes Wholesale Customer-funded extensions the customer's sole property.
Network Operator is "required to periodically update or upgrade" without any stated frequency or standard beyond "carrier-grade quality and reliability."

The upgrade obligation is capped by the CAPEX Fund balance, yet Section 4.9.1 makes Network Operator responsible for all costs of compliance with the Agreement and Section 4.11.1 requires carrier class standards regardless of funding.

Tasks "whether or not specifically described in this Agreement" are deemed included if "required for the proper performance and provision of the Services," a self-expanding scope with no external limit.
Two ceilings are imposed at once — the Price Caps and 85% of the then-current Price Schedule — without saying which governs if the Price Schedule falls below the Caps.
The Price Caps are located in "Exhibit F," but the Agreement's exhibit list assigns Price Caps to Exhibit D and the EOPSS/ITD Master Services Agreement to Exhibit F.

The present assignment of Third Party Service Provider contracts effective on termination must be read with Section 12.10, which bars assignment without consent, and with Section 8.5.1's transfer-on-request mechanism.
"[A]t a the price of $60/mile/strand/month" is garbled, and the fixed price is immediately qualified by "as the same may be adjusted from time to time," leaving unclear whether the figure binds.
"The Parties will develop guidelines" with an "expectation" of accommodation and "favorable consideration" states no enforceable standard for approving non-standard leases.

The Price Caps are said to be "set forth in Exhibit F," but the exhibit list places Price Caps at Exhibit D, and amendment "pursuant to ARTICLE 6" conflicts with Section 6.2's requirement of express written approval of both parties.

The first sentence makes every annual update "subject to approval by MTC," while the second implies only increases exceeding CPI require MTC approval; the two sentences cannot both be given full effect.

The prohibition on Network Operator providing Retail Services is circular given Section 2.57, which defines Retail Service as service provided by a Third Party Service Provider, i.e. by definition someone other than Network Operator (Section 2.64).
The cost list closes with "all other operating and monitoring expenses contemplated by this Agreement," a catch-all whose reach against the enumerated items is open to ejusdem generis argument.

The estimate is made "as a precondition to exercising the right to object set forth in Section 4.9.2.5," but Section 4.9.2.5 creates no right to object — it creates only a credit against revenue sharing.
The credit is measured by cost incurred "as a result of MTC's agreeing to the contractual term objected to," though this Section describes no objection procedure at all.

The reduction is "in proportion to the average shortfall (from 90%) in the percentage of CAIs that have been connected as of the end of each week," a formula that does not state how the proportion is computed or applied to quarterly payments.
The relief depends on delay being "attributable to MTC" or third parties, which must be read with Section 2.7's right of MTC to revise the CAI list that fixes the 90% denominator.
Section 2.4 defines the Annual Plan as the plan submitted "pursuant to Section 4.9.2," whereas the obligation actually sits here in Section 4.9.3.2.

The fee is described as paid "annually in four (4) equal parts at the beginning of each calendar quarter," and the "Year" units are keyed to the Effective Date while the Term is measured from the Commencement Date.

Because Section 3.1 runs the Term to ten years after the Commencement Date, which Section 2.8 allows to be up to thirty months after the Effective Date, the ten-year fee table can expire before the Term does.
The formula literally multiplies the Year 10 fee by "100 plus the increase in CPI ... stated as a percentage," which produces a hundredfold result unless the worked example is used to correct it.
Payment is due within 45 days after Network Operator's fiscal year, while Section 4.9.8 states that all payments to MTC "shall be paid quarterly unless another payment schedule is specified herein."
"[A]mounts reasonably required for the purposes of the Fund" sets no measure for when MTC may divert excess funds to other uses.
Payment is annual here, while Section 4.9.8 provides that payments to MTC are quarterly unless another schedule is specified; the schedules must be harmonised.
The default quarterly rule must be reconciled with the annual payment dates in Sections 4.9.5 and 4.9.7 and the quarterly CAPEX payment in Section 4.9.6.

The restriction stacks two conditions — a stated duration over two years and IFRS revenue recognition more than two years after receipt — so it is unclear whether both must be satisfied or the second merely explains the first.
"[T]he standards for carrier class networks" is an undefined external benchmark, layered on specifications "to be contained or incorporated" in a contract not attached.
"MTC may not prevent Network Operator from performing maintenance that Network Operator deems necessary" is a subjective standard placed in the middle of MTC notice and presence rights.
That sentence sits uneasily with Section 4.11.7, which subjects Network Operator's preventative and restorative procedures to MTC's approval, and with MTC's oversight role under Section 4.1.
"[W]orkmanlike care" is an undefined standard sitting alongside the stricter obligations elsewhere in Article 4.

"[A]s quickly as possible (allowing for delays caused by circumstances beyond the reasonable control of Network Operator)" states no measurable response time against the SLA specifications it references.
"[F]ull compliance with all Network Policies" is an absolute duty measured against a set that Section 2.44 permits MTC to enlarge with "any additional policies reasonably required by MTC."
Performance is measured against "the SLA the Parties are in the process of completing," a document that does not yet exist and is not attached as Exhibit E.
The cross-reference to Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5 is misplaced: those provisions govern MTC's agreements with third parties and cost credits, not completion of the SLA.
The parties "will review and agree to commercially reasonable changes" — an agreement to agree with no fallback if they do not.
"[A]ll remunerative payments" is an unusual and undefined phrase for what must be paid when an audit shows the accounting is not correct.
"[U]nless expressly constructed otherwise" is a mechanical error for "construed," and it is the very words that carve out the exception to the no-leasehold rule.
The denial of any interest in the MTC Network must be squared with Section 3.6.1, which grants Network Operator an IRU lease of dark fiber, and with Section 4.5.4's carve-out.

Security policies must be "in line with industry best practices" and "no less stringent than the then-current requirements of MassDOT, ITD and EOPSS," standards set outside the instrument and capable of changing.

The warranty extends back to January 1, 2005 and covers "any criminal proceeding or investigation" against any officer, director or Affiliate, a sweep whose breach threshold is not qualified by materiality.
"[S]ubstantially equivalent" services "in other settings and circumstances" gives no measurable content to the experience warranty.
"[S]elf-dealing" is undefined and the duty to "ensure that the interests of MTC ... are protected in all transactions" reads as an open-ended fiduciary-like standard.

That protective duty is in tension with Section 4.5.5 and Section 2.43, which expressly contemplate Network Operator building and profiting from its own Network Extensions connected to the MTC Network.

Compliance is promised with Article 5 of a Master Services Agreement that the provision itself says is "currently being negotiated," and the finalization cross-reference to Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5 concerns cost estimates and credits, not this agreement's contents.

The representation that all required insurance "has" been taken out as of the Effective Date sits against Section 10.3.3, which allows thirty days after the Effective Date to furnish certificates and later procurement of some coverages.
An absolute covenant to "ensure that the MTC Network is and remains" compliant is difficult to square with Section 4.2.1, under which MTC alone is responsible for design and construction decisions.
Purpose (iv) makes the IPT a dispute-resolution body, but Section 6.1.2 gives MTC both a majority-chaired seat and the chair, while Section 11.1.2 assumes the IPT may fail to resolve and escalates.

A five-member body with two representatives per Party plus an EOPSS/ITD member is charged under Section 11.1.3 with acting by "unanimous vote" to stay dispute deadlines, and no voting rule is otherwise given.
Meeting "at least once a year" is hard to reconcile with Section 11.1.1.2, which requires the IPT to meet "as often as necessary" within the fifteen-day dispute window of Section 11.1.2.
The section requires a "threshold determination" and then a "mutual determination," without saying what happens if the Parties disagree on whether an amendment is needed.
The obligation to "promptly deliver to the requesting party any and all Confidential Information" on demand "at any time" is unqualified and would strip the holder of information it needs to perform.
That return-on-demand right cannot easily be squared with Section 7.3.4, which fixes return and deletion at termination and permits retention of customer information required by law.
The indemnity is given "[t]o the maximum extent required by law" rather than permitted by law, which as written may promise nothing at all.

The Section turns on "Applicable Third Party," "Written Materials" and "Governmental Authority," capitalized terms not defined in Article 2, which states that all capitalized terms take their meanings there.
The carve-outs use "Applicable Third Party" and "Governmental Authority," terms not defined in Article 2, and refer to the "General Counsel" without identifying whose.

Section 8.1.2 permits termination for "a series of non-material or persistent breaches" having "a material and significant adverse impact," a standard with no cure right and no measure of how many or how significant.
Section 8.1.2 offers no notice or cure period at all, while Section 8.1.1 gives thirty days for a material breach, so the lesser breaches carry the harsher consequence.

Notice must be given "not later than fourteen (14) days after the notice of the occurrence of such change of control," though no provision requires Network Operator to give notice of a change of control.

The charge is calculated by "increasing the percentage of Network Revenue owed ... under Section 4.9.5" by half a percent, without saying which of the three tiered percentages is increased or whether all are.

The escalator runs from "beyond the initial thirty (30) days" while Section 8.1.1 makes the thirty-day cure period the trigger for termination rights, leaving the start date of the charge contestable.
"[D]isruption to the basic functioning of more than fifty percent (50%) of the MTC Network" gives no unit of measurement — mileage, strands, customers or revenue.
"[B]asic functioning of one or more elements" and an extension "by the period of time reasonably required" leave both the trigger and the relief undefined.
The Term is "deemed" not to expire until transfer assistance "is completed or MTC waives the requirement," giving one party open-ended control over when the contract ends.

That deeming provision cannot be reconciled with Section 3.1, which fixes expiry at the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date, or with Section 8.6, which gives Network Operator its own termination rights.

A one-year cap on the extension of the effective date of termination is difficult to square with Section 8.4.1, under which the Term is not deemed to expire at all until transfer assistance is complete.
Transfer or assignment is to occur "on mutually acceptable terms and conditions," which leaves the obligation dependent on a further agreement that may never be reached.

Network Operator's termination right is undercut by Section 11.2, which requires continued performance while a dispute is resolved "unless otherwise directed by MTC," and by Section 8.4.1's deeming provision.

The indemnity covers claims "arising out of" five enumerated categories while limb (d) reaches acts causing MTC to breach an agreement with "any other person relating to the MTC Network," a catch-all of uncertain reach.

MTC's indemnity omits the bodily injury and property damage limb given to MTC in Section 9.1(a), an asymmetry that would be construed against the drafter if the omission were argued to be inadvertent.
Notice must be given "immediately" of any occurrence "which would be the basis of an Indemnified Claim," with no stated consequence for late notice.

Requiring written approval of both Parties for "[a]ny settlement" gives the Indemnified Party a veto that sits oddly with the Indemnifying Party's "primary responsibility for the conduct" of the proceeding under Section 9.3.
"As and when required" is an undefined trigger for the automobile coverage obligation.
The scope of the property coverage is left to the Parties to "confer" and "use commercially reasonable efforts to agree" upon, so the obligation is an agreement to agree.

Section 8.1.1 makes a breach under Section 10.3.3 terminable on ten days' cure, and Section 10.3.3 excepts "as set forth in Section 10.2.1," so an unagreed coverage level feeds directly into a termination trigger.
"Where possible" and "commensurate with the value of the assets in service" leave the required aggregate limit unascertainable.

Rental loss insurance is required only "[s]ubject to such further determination as to commercially reasonable amounts, timing, deductibles, and terms," leaving the obligation contingent on further agreement.
Section 2.45 and Section 4.11.8.2 treat rental loss proceeds as Network Revenue on which fees are owed, yet whether such coverage exists at all is left to later determination here.
The last sentence's phrase "within five (5) days of requiring such insurance" is ambiguous as to whether the trigger is the need for the insurance or its procurement.

A breach of this Section is singled out in Section 8.1.1 for a ten-day cure and termination, yet its opening words except whatever is "set forth in Section 10.2.1," which is itself an agreement to agree.
"[C]ommercially reasonable types and amounts of liability insurance coverage" for subcontractors is left to be documented without a stated standard or approver.
The cross-reference to "agreements ... within the scope of Section 4.1" is imprecise: Section 4.1 lists Network Operator responsibilities generally rather than identifying any set of MTC agreements.
"Any dispute ... with respect to the interpretation of any provision" or "with respect to the performance" is a broad scope whose reach over non-contractual or tort claims is not addressed.

Escalation is triggered fifteen days "after the date of receipt by the other Party" of the notice, but resolution is due thirty days "after the receipt" of the same notice, giving the officers only the remainder of the period.
"Except in the case of an emergency" excuses exhaustion of the pre-arbitration steps without defining what an emergency is or who decides.

The stipulation that arbitration is "a condition precedent to any suit" sits against Section 11.1.4, which allows court action for injunctive relief "[n]otwithstanding any other provision of this Section" at any time.
Court action is permitted "if the dispute resolution processes ... would permit or cause irreparable injury" — a self-judging condition with no standard for who determines it or when.
This carve-out and the condition precedent to suit in Section 11.1.3 pull in opposite directions on when a party may go to court before arbitrating.

"[U]nless otherwise directed by MTC" gives one party a unilateral power to switch off continued performance, with no indication whether it can direct only its own or also the other Party's obligations to stop.

Requiring performance to continue during a dispute cannot be squared with Section 8.6, which lets Network Operator terminate for MTC's uncured material breach, nor with Section 8.4.1's deeming of the Term as continuing.
The merger is limited to "the Services and matters addressed therein," leaving open what else, such as the parent guaranty required by Section 12.14, survives outside the integration.

Several exhibits the Agreement treats as operative (Exhibit E's SLA, the finalised Network Policies) do not exist at signature, which is hard to square with an entire-agreement clause allowing change only by signed writing.
"Time is of the essence" is placed immediately beside a general excuse for nonperformance caused by the other Party, and the two sentences pull against each other without a priority rule.

Naming only Articles 9 and 11 alongside a general catch-all invites an expressio unius argument that other obligations, such as the Article 7 confidentiality duties expressed to apply after termination, do not survive.
Article 7 and Section 3.6.1.8's twenty-five-year dark fiber lease are expressly post-termination in operation but are not listed here, so the survival clause and those provisions must be reconciled.
Interest is keyed to "the rediscount rate then charged by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston," a rate that may not be published under that name.
An invalid provision is "deemed to be restated to reflect the Parties' original intentions," which asks the reader to rewrite rather than sever the term.

The permitted assignees are "another entity of the Commonwealth, a subsidiary of MTC or a special purpose entity," yet the notice sentence speaks of assignment "to an Affiliate," a different and defined category.

The denial of third-party rights is hard to reconcile with Section 10.3, which requires MassDOT and its bond trustees to be named additional insureds, and with Article 9's indemnity in favour of non-party Indemnified Parties.
Clause (e) makes email notice effective only "if sent by email and one of the delivery methods in (a) through (d) above," which is ambiguous as to whether email alone ever suffices.
The address block is headed "[f]or termination, breach or default" notices only, leaving no stated address for the many other notices the Agreement requires under Section 12.12.1.

The general duty not to withhold consent unreasonably conflicts with the several provisions conferring unqualified discretion, notably Section 2.7 ("MTC's sole discretion"), Section 4.9.7 and Section 8.2.

The proviso reads "provided, however, that Network Operator shall be subject to any application or access fees," which as a proviso favouring Network Operator appears to have dropped a negative and reverses the intended allocation.

The closing sentence makes Network Operator solely responsible for approvals "for any Alterations to be done by or on behalf of MTC," which is difficult to square with Section 4.2.1's allocation of construction responsibility to MTC.
"[A]ll reasonable efforts to limit the rights and obligations of Network Operator" so it avoids subrecipient status is an open-ended instruction that could cut against express obligations elsewhere.

The Agreement becomes binding "only upon condition" that a guaranty "in a form acceptable to MTC" with a limit "no less than four million" dollars is delivered, leaving both the form and the operation of the condition in one party's hands.
A guaranty by a non-party is made a condition of the Agreement's binding effect, which must be read against Section 12.11's disclaimer of third-party rights and Section 12.1's integration clause.
